'''Tyler Volk''' is a [[Emeritus|Professor Emeritus]] of [[Environmental studies|Environmental Studies]] and [[Biology]] at [[New York University]] (NYU). His areas of interest include environmental challenges to global prosperity, global changes in [[Carbon dioxide|CO<sub>2</sub>]], [[Biosphere|biosphere theory]], and the role of [[Earthlife|life]] in [[Earth]]'s dynamics.<ref name=":0">{{cite web
 | url = http://as.nyu.edu/environment.html  | title = NYU Department of Environmental Studies}}</ref> He first attended the [[University of Michigan]], graduating with a [[Bachelor's degree|Bachelors]] in [[Architecture]] in 1971; he later graduated from NYU with a [[Master's degree|Masters]] in [[Applied science|Applied Sciences]] in 1982 and a [[Doctor of Philosophy|PhD]] in Applied Sciences in 1984.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Tyler Volk |url=https://as.nyu.edu/faculty/tyler-volk.html?challenge=d06e90d7-4d8f-4b88-9d8c-10b73beb60f1 |access-date= |website=NYU Arts & Sciences: Faculty}}</ref>

==Environmental studies and teaching==
Volk worked on the planning and development of the Environmental Studies Program with [[Dale Jamieson]] and Christopher Schlottmann, launching it in 2007; the program became a department in NYU’s Faculty of Arts and Science in 2014.<ref name=":0" /> Volk was awarded NYU’s “Golden Dozen” teaching award in both 2004 and 2008.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Past Recipients |url=https://cas.nyu.edu/teaching-awards/past-recipients.html |access-date=2026-04-30 |website=cas.nyu.edu |language=en-US}}</ref> Volk also received a Distinguished Teaching Award in 2009.<ref>{{Cite web |title=2008-2009 Distinguished Teaching Award Recipients |url=https://www.nyu.edu/en/academics/awards-and-highlights/university-distinguishedteachingawards/past-recipients/2008-2009-distinguished-teaching-award-recipients.html |access-date=2026-04-30 |website=www.nyu.edu |language=en}}</ref>

==Biosphere science==
Volk's research explores Earth's biosphere, modeling the global [[carbon cycle]], and quantifying the biological and physical impacts from the ocean and biosphere on it.<ref>{{Citation
| last1       = Volk
| first1      = Tyler
| last2      = Hoffert
| first2     = Martin
| date       = 1985
| contribution = Ocean carbon pumps: analysis of relative strengths and efficiencies in ocean-driven atmospheric CO<sub>2</sub> changes
| title = The Carbon Cycle and Atmospheric CO<sub>2</sub>: Natural Variations Archean to Present
| editor = E. T. Sundquist and W. S. Broecker
| volume     = Geophysical Monograph 32
| pages      = 99–110
| publisher = American Geophysical Union, Wash., D.C.}}</ref>

In 2000, Volk served on the [[American Geophysical Union]]'s Chapman Conference on the [[Gaia hypothesis|Gaia Hypothesis]] program committee in [[Valencia]], [[Spain]]. His presentation, ''“Gaia is life in a wasteworld of by-products”'', was published in 2004.<ref>Volk, T. (2004). “Gaia is life in a wasteworld of by-products,“ in ''Scientists Debate Gaia,'' S. H. Schneider, et al. (eds.), Cambridge, MA: MIT Press, pp. 27—36.</ref> He has debated [[James Lovelock]], [[Tim Lenton]] and David Wilkinson on various concepts relating to the Gaia Hypothesis.<ref>{{cite journal
| last       = Volk
| first      = Tyler
| date       = 2003
| title      = Seeing deeper into Gaia theory: A reply to Lovelock's response
| journal    = Climatic Change
| volume     = 57
| pages      = 5–7
| doi        = 10.1023/a:1022193813703
}}</ref> Volk also publicly debated Axel Kleidon on the role of [[entropy]] in the [[biosphere]].<ref>{{cite journal
| last       = Volk
| first      = Tyler
| date       = 2007
| title      = The properties of organisms are not tunable parameters selected because they create maximum entropy production on the biosphere scale: A by-product framework in response to Kleidon
| journal    = Climatic Change
| volume     = 85
| issue = 3–4
| pages      = 251–258
| doi        = 10.1007/s10584-007-9319-3
}}
</ref>

==NASA advanced life support==
Volk developed math models for element cycling in "[[Controlled ecological life-support system|closed ecological life support systems]]" (CELSS) at [[NASA]]<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Macelroy |first=Robert D. |last2=Thompson |first2=Brad G. |last3=Tibbitts |first3=Theodore W. |last4=Volk |first4=Tyler |date=1989-12-01 |title=Controlled Ecological Life Support Systems: Natural and Artificial Ecosystems |url=https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/19910015430 |language=en}}</ref> and remained active in the subfield of advanced life support from 1986 to 1998. He and colleague John Rummel developed early computer models that demonstrated the chemical transformations of [[Agriculture|crop production]], [[Metabolism|human metabolism]], and waste processing.<ref>{{cite journal
| last1       = Volk
| first1      = Tyler
| last2      = Rummel
| first2     = John D.
| date       = 1987
| title      = Mass balances for a biological life support system simulation model
| journal    = Advances in Space Research
| volume     = 7
| issue      = 4
| pages      = (4)141-(4)148
| doi = 10.1016/0273-1177(87)90045-7
| pmid = 11537263
| hdl = 2060/19880002890
| hdl-access= free
}}</ref> Volk later studied crop growth and development for enhanced productivity, collaborating with crop physiologists [[Bruce Bugbee]] of [[Utah State University]], Raymond Wheeler of the NASA [[Kennedy Space Center]],<ref>{{cite journal
| last1       = Volk
| first1      = Tyler
| last2      = Bugbee
| first2     = Bruce
| last3      = Wheeler
| first3     = Raymond M.
| date       = 1995
| title      = An approach to crop modeling with the energy cascade
| journal    = Life Support & Biosphere Science
| volume     = 1
| pages      = 119–127
}}</ref> and Ph.D. students Francesco Tubiello and James Cavazonni at NYU.<ref>{{cite journal
| last1       = Tubiello
| first1      = Francesco N.
| last2      = Volk
| first2     = Tyler
| last3      = Bugbee
| first3     = Bruce
| date       = 1997
| title      = Diffuse light and wheat radiation-use efficiency in a controlled environment
| journal    = Life Support & Biosphere Science
| volume     = 4
| pages      = 77–85
}}</ref>

==Books==
Tyler Volk has authored seven [[book]]s, including ''CO<sub>2</sub> Rising: The World’s Greatest Environmental Challenge'',<ref>{{Cite book|title=CO<sub>2</sub> Rising: The World's Greatest Environmental Challenge|last=Volk|first=Tyler|publisher=The MIT Press|year=2008|isbn=978-0-262-22083-5|location=USA|url-access=registration|url=https://archive.org/details/corisingworldsgr0000volk}}</ref> ''What is Death?: A Scientist Looks at the Cycle of Life'',<ref>{{Cite book|title=What is Death?: A Scientist Looks at the Cycle of Life|last=Volk|first=Tyler|publisher=John Wiley & Sons|year=2002|isbn=0-471-37544-6|location=USA}}</ref> ''Gaia's Body: Toward a Physiology of Earth'',<ref>{{Cite book|title=Gaia's Body: Toward a Physiology of the Earth|last=Volk|first=Tyler|publisher=Copernicus Books/Springer-Verlag|year=1998|isbn=0-262-72042-6|location=USA}}</ref> and ''Metapatterns: Across Space, Time, and Mind''.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Metapatterns: Across Space, Time, and Mind|last=Volk|first=Tyler|publisher=Columbia University Press|year=1996|isbn=9780231067515}}</ref>

In 2017, he published ''Quarks to Culture: How We Came to Be,''<ref>{{Cite book|title=Quarks to Culture: How We Came to Be.|last=Volk|first=Tyler|publisher=Columbia University Press|date=May 2017|isbn=978-0231179607|location=USA}}</ref> which explores what Tyler Volk calls the "grand sequence", which outlines a series of evolutionary levels from [[Elementary particle|elementary quanta]] to globalized [[human civilization]]. The book was reviewed in ''Science'' in January 2018.<ref>{{cite journal
| last       = Wood
| first      = Barry
| date       = 19 Jan 2018
| title      = Quarks, culture, combogenesis
| url        = http://blogs.sciencemag.org/books/2018/01/16/quarks-to-culture/
| journal    = Science
| volume     = 359
| issue      = 6373
| pages      = 281
| doi        = 10.1126/science.aar8252
| url-access= subscription
}}</ref>
